learn.text: Authors don't always tell us everything. Inference means using clues in the text plus what you already know to work out what is not said directly. Always point to the evidence.

visual.title: The Audition
visual.text: Ines stood outside the hall door for the third time, her violin case gripped so tightly that her knuckles turned white. Inside, someone was playing the piece she had practised every evening for a month. She checked her watch, smoothed her hair, and took a long, slow breath. When the door finally opened and a voice called, "Next!", she didn't move for a moment. Then she lifted her chin and walked in.

misconceptions.description: Only accepts what is stated directly, missing implied meaning.
misconceptions.remedy: Ask: what do these actions suggest about how the character feels?

misconceptions.description: Picks an inference that sounds possible but isn't supported by the text.
misconceptions.remedy: Every inference needs a clue you can point to.

items.prompt: How is Ines feeling at the start?
hints: Look at how she holds the violin case.
items.explanation: Gripping the case so tightly her knuckles turned white, and standing outside 'for the third time', suggest she is nervous.

items.prompt: Which clue shows Ines has worked hard to prepare?

options.label: She practised every evening for a month

items.explanation: Practising every evening for a month shows real effort and preparation.

items.prompt: Why does she take 'a long, slow breath'?
hints: What do people do when they feel nervous?
items.explanation: People often take slow breaths to calm nerves. It fits the other clues that she is nervous.

items.prompt: What is most likely happening in the hall?

options.label: People are performing to try to be chosen

items.explanation: The title 'The Audition' and the call of 'Next!' show people are taking turns to be judged.

items.prompt: What does 'she lifted her chin and walked in' suggest?

options.label: She chose to be brave despite her nerves
She thinks she is better than everyone

hints: She didn't move at first. Then what changed?
Lifting your chin can show determination.
items.explanation: After hesitating, she lifts her chin — a sign of gathering courage, not arrogance.

items.prompt: Which word best describes Ines overall?
hints: Think about her month of practice and her final action.
She is nervous but does it anyway.
items.explanation: She practised for a month and walked in despite her nerves: she is determined.

learn.text: The main idea is what a paragraph is mostly about. Details support it. A good test: could the main idea be a title for the whole paragraph? A detail only covers one part.

visual.title: City Bees
visual.text: Bees are not only found in the countryside. In many European cities, beekeepers now keep hives on rooftops, balconies and even on top of hotels. City parks, gardens and street trees provide a surprising variety of flowers. Some studies have found that city bees can produce as much honey as country bees, partly because cities often use fewer pesticides on gardens. However, experts warn that too many hives in one area can leave too little food for wild bees.

misconceptions.description: Chooses a single detail as the main idea.
misconceptions.remedy: Does it cover the whole paragraph, or just one sentence?

misconceptions.description: Chooses an idea far bigger than the text (e.g. 'All about insects').
misconceptions.remedy: The main idea should match this text, not the whole topic.

items.prompt: What is the paragraph mostly about?

options.label: Bees can live and do well in cities

hints: What does the first sentence say?
Which answer could be a title?
items.explanation: The whole paragraph is about bees living in cities. Hotels are one detail; 'all insects' is too broad.

items.prompt: Which is a supporting detail?

options.label: Hives are kept on rooftops and balconies
Bees are not only found in the countryside

hints: Which one is a specific fact?
items.explanation: Rooftop and balcony hives are an example supporting the main idea.

items.prompt: According to the text, why might city bees make as much honey?

options.label: Gardens often use fewer pesticides, and there's a variety of flowers

hints: Which reason is actually in the text?
items.explanation: The text mentions a variety of flowers and fewer pesticides.

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the last sentence?

options.label: To add a warning or other side
To say bees should leave cities

items.explanation: 'However' introduces a caution: too many hives can harm wild bees.

items.prompt: Which is the best one-sentence summary?

options.label: City beekeeping can be successful, but too many hives may harm wild bees.
Honey is made by bees from flowers in many places around the world.

hints: A summary includes the main idea and the key twist.
Which one mentions both success and the warning?
items.explanation: Option A covers the main idea and the warning. B is a detail; C is too broad.

items.prompt: Which title fits best?
hints: The title should match the main idea.
items.explanation: 'Buzzing Above the Streets' captures bees living in cities.

learn.text: A fact can be checked and proved true or false. An opinion is what someone thinks or feels; people can disagree. Opinion clues: best, worst, beautiful, boring, should, I think. Adverts often mix both!
learn.example: Fact: The Vistula is the longest river in Poland. Opinion: The Vistula is the most beautiful river.

misconceptions.description: Labels an opinion as fact because they agree with it.
misconceptions.remedy: Could someone reasonably disagree? Then it's an opinion, even if you agree.

misconceptions.description: Thinks any sentence with a number is a fact.
misconceptions.remedy: Look for judgement words. 'The 3 best games' is still an opinion.

items.prompt: 'Water freezes at 0 °C.' Fact or opinion?
items.explanation: It can be tested and proved, so it's a fact.

items.prompt: 'Pizza is the best food in the world.' Fact or opinion?
items.explanation: 'Best' is a judgement. Others might prefer pierogi or dosa!

items.prompt: 'These are the 3 most exciting films of the year.' Fact or opinion?
hints: Ignore the number for a moment.
items.explanation: Even with a number, 'most exciting' is a judgement, so it's an opinion.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a fact?

options.label: Our school has the friendliest teachers.

hints: Which could be checked in records?
items.explanation: The building date can be checked. The others are opinions.

items.prompt: Advert: 'SuperCrunch has 12 g of sugar per bowl. It's the tastiest breakfast ever!' Which part is a fact?
hints: Which part could you check on the box?
items.explanation: The sugar amount can be checked. 'Tastiest ever' is an opinion designed to persuade.

items.prompt: Why do adverts mix facts and opinions?

options.label: Facts build trust, opinions persuade you to buy

hints: What is an advert trying to do?
Facts make the opinions sound more believable.
items.explanation: Real facts make the advert seem trustworthy, so the opinions feel more convincing. Spotting this makes you a critical reader.

learn.text: Writers paint pictures with words. A simile compares using 'like' or 'as' (as quiet as a mouse). A metaphor says something IS something else (the classroom was a zoo). Personification gives human actions to things (the wind whispered).
learn.example: Simile: Her smile was like sunshine. Metaphor: Her smile was sunshine. Personification: The sun smiled down.

misconceptions.remedy: Ask: is this really possible? If not, what picture is the writer creating?
Look for 'like' or 'as'. If it's there, it's a simile.

items.prompt: 'The baby slept like a log.' What is this?
hints: It compares the baby to a log.
items.explanation: It uses 'like' to compare, so it's a simile.

items.prompt: 'The old door groaned as it opened.' What is this?
items.explanation: The door is given a human action (groaning), so it's personification.

items.prompt: 'Dad is a bear in the morning.' What does it mean?

options.label: Dad is grumpy in the morning

hints: What are bears like when woken up?
items.explanation: It's a metaphor: Dad acts grumpy, like a woken bear.

items.prompt: Which is a metaphor?

options.label: The snow was a white blanket.
The snow was like a white blanket.

hints: A metaphor says something IS something else.
items.explanation: 'The snow was a white blanket' says the snow IS a blanket. B is a simile; C is literal.

items.prompt: 'Time crawled during the long maths test.' What effect does 'crawled' create?

options.label: There was a baby in the room

items.explanation: Crawling is slow, so the writer shows that time seemed to pass very slowly.

items.prompt: Which sentence best shows a nervous character using a simile?

options.label: Her heart raced like a galloping horse.

hints: It must be a simile: like or as.
It should show nerves, not just tell.
items.explanation: A uses 'like' and shows nerves through a vivid image. C is a metaphor; B just tells.

learn.text: A prefix goes at the start of a word and changes its meaning: un- (not), re- (again), pre- (before), mis- (wrongly). A suffix goes at the end: -ful (full of), -less (without), -able (can be). Knowing these unlocks thousands of words.
learn.example: un + believ(e) + able = unbelievable: cannot be believed

misconceptions.description: Applies the wrong meaning to a prefix or suffix.
misconceptions.remedy: Learn the core meanings: un = not, re = again, less = without.
-ful means full of; -less means without. They are often opposites.

items.prompt: What does 'rebuild' mean?
items.explanation: re- means again, so rebuild means build again.

items.prompt: Which prefix makes 'happy' mean 'not happy'?
items.explanation: un- means not: unhappy.

items.prompt: A 'fearless' explorer is...
items.explanation: Fearless means without fear: very brave.

items.prompt: What does 'misread' mean?
items.explanation: mis- means wrongly, so misread means to read something wrongly.

items.prompt: Build a word meaning 'cannot be predicted'.
items.explanation: un (not) + predict + able (can be) = unpredictable.

items.prompt: 'The medieval town was pre-industrial.' What does pre-industrial mean?
items.explanation: pre- means before, so pre-industrial means before industry developed.
